title: Particles: mah, téh, atuh, waé
title_target: Kecap panganteb: mah, téh, atuh, waé
goal: Master the little words that have no dictionary meaning but set the whole feel of a sentence — the part that most clearly separates real speakers from people reading out of a book.
bekal: *mah* and *téh*: the two most frequent particles, and the two most often confused
*pisan* and *teuing*: two intensifiers with very different tones

dialogs.title: Paguneman — Teased for not getting it
dialogs.intro: Late afternoon on the porch. Rani shows Sari her notes and complains that she understands every word but not the sentences.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.text: Sar, kuring téh bingung. Naon ari mah jeung téh?
lines.id: Sar, I'm confused. What are mah and téh?
lines.literal: Sar, I [téh] confused. what [ari] mah and téh?

lines.speaker: Sari:
lines.text: Hahaha. Éta mah nu paling hésé, tapi paling penting.
lines.id: Hahaha. That's the hardest part — but the most important.
lines.literal: hahaha. that [mah] which most hard, but most important.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.text: Tuh, kakara ogé maké dua kali dina hiji kalimah.
lines.id: See, you just used it twice in one sentence.
lines.literal: see, just-now also used two times in one sentence.

lines.speaker: Sari:
lines.text: Kieu. Mah téh keur ngabédakeun. Kuring mah teu bisa — hartina batur mah bisa.
lines.id: Look. Mah is for contrasting. Kuring mah teu bisa — means other people can.
lines.literal: like-this. mah [téh] for differentiating. I [mah] not can — meaning-its others [mah] can.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.text: Ooh, jadi kawas "kalau saya sih" kitu?
lines.id: Oh, so it's like "kalau saya sih" — "well, as for me"?

lines.speaker: Sari:
lines.text: Persis! Ari téh mah nunjuk barang nu geus dipikanyaho duaan.
lines.id: Exactly! And téh points to something you both already know about.
lines.literal: exactly! as-for téh [mah] points thing which already known by-both.

lines.speaker: Sari:
lines.text: Buku téh mana? Hartina buku nu urang duaan geus nyaho. Lain buku sagala rupa.
lines.id: Buku téh mana? That means the book we both know about. Not just any book.
lines.literal: book [téh] where? meaning-its book which we both already know. not book all kinds.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.text: Kawas "tuh" atawa "itu lho" nya. Terus atuh?

lines.speaker: Sari:
lines.text: Atuh mah pikeun ngalemeskeun. Hayu atuh — hartina hayu dong, ulah kitu waé.
lines.id: Atuh is for softening. Hayu atuh — means come on, don't just sit there.
lines.literal: atuh [mah] for softening. come-on atuh — meaning-its come-on [dong], don't like-that just.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.text: Sigana kuring kudu ngadéngékeun waé heula, ulah loba tanya.
lines.id: I think I'd better just listen for a while, and not ask so much.
lines.literal: seems I must listen just first, don't many ask.

lines.speaker: Sari:
lines.text: Heueuh. Ieu mah teu bisa diapalkeun, kudu karasa. Sabulan ogé apal geuning.
lines.id: Yep. You can't memorize this, you have to feel it. In a month you'll have it, you'll see.
lines.literal: yes. this [mah] not can memorized, must felt. one-month also memorized [geuning].

notes: **Mah** puts the topic in the spotlight and **always** carries a hidden contrast. *Kuring mah teu bisa* doesn't just mean "I can't"; it means "well, *I* can't — others might". English gets close with "as for me…", "me, I…", or a stressed *I*.

**Téh** marks something **already known to both** speaker and listener. It works rather like English *the* (as opposed to *a*), or "that … you know". *Bukuna mana?* = where's a book, any book; *buku téh mana?* = where's the book (we both know about)?
**Atuh** softens, coaxes, and pleads a little. It never changes the meaning, only the temperature of the sentence. *Hayu* = come on; *hayu atuh* = oh, come on!
**Waé / baé** = just, only; or all the time. *Ieu waé* = just this one; *ulin waé* = playing all the time. *Baé* sounds gentler and more old-fashioned.
**Kawas** = like, as (loma); the lemes form is **sapertos**. It's not the same as *siga*, which is closer to "resembling": *kawas kuring* = like me (as I do); *siga kuring* = looks like me.
**Diapalkeun** from *apal* (to know by heart). The prefix *di-* + suffix *-keun* makes a passive: "made memorized". The *di-…-keun* pattern appears often from Unit 10 on.
**Karasa** from *rasa* (feel), with the prefix *ka-* meaning "happens by itself": *karasa* = can be felt, *katingali* = can be seen, *kadéngé* = can be heard.

grammars.title: Nine particles and where they go
body: A particle always comes **after** the word it applies to, never before. Position decides meaning: *kuring mah teu bisa* (well, I can't) is not the same as *kuring teu bisa mah* — the second sounds wrong.

Example
Feels like
rows: oh, there is one after all!
that one, the one we discussed
where's that book, the one we said?

after: Two particles can sit side by side, and very often do: *ieu mah téh…*, *éta mah geuning…*, *hayu atuh euy!*. The order isn't free — *mah* always comes before *téh*, and *euy* always goes at the very end.

⚠️ The most common learner mistake: sprinkling *atuh* and *mah* into every sentence in the belief that this is what makes it sound Sundanese. The result sounds like an impression, not speech. One particle every two or three sentences is plenty; the rest can be plain.

These particles **can't be learned from a table** — they go in through your ears. The fastest way: listen to one Sundanese conversation a day for two weeks without trying to use them at all. After that they'll start coming out in the right places on their own.

sections.title: Mah versus téh — side by side

blocks.text: These two are mixed up most often, and the difference shows most clearly when the same sentence is used with each:

head: Sentence
Meaning
What it implies
rows: the rice we were just talking about

blocks.text: A practical tip: if in English you would naturally say **"well, as for…"** or stress the word to contrast it, use *mah*. If you would naturally say **"the… (we mentioned)"** or **"that… you know"**, use *téh*. It isn't perfect, but it works for nine out of ten A1 sentences.

blocks.title: Everyday sentences with mah and téh
items: **Abdi mah nembé sumping.** — I've only just arrived, myself.
**Ieu téh sabaraha?** — How much is this one?
**Bandung mah tiis.** — Bandung, now — it's cool.
**Kuring mah tara ka ditu.** — Me, I never go there.
**Hargana téh awis pisan.** — The price is really high.

sections.title: Pisan, teuing, and how to intensify

blocks.text: Sundanese has several intensifiers, and picking the wrong one can turn praise into a complaint.
⚠️ **Teuing** is always negative when it means "too". *Ngeunah teuing* sounds odd — you're complaining that something is too tasty. To praise, use **pisan** or **mani**.

**Teuing** has a second, completely different meaning: **no idea**. On its own or with *duka*, it becomes an answer: *Duka teuing.* = "Who knows — I've no idea." It's a very common and very useful reply — much softer than *teu terang* ("I don't know"), which sounds like it ends the conversation.

blocks.title: Superlatives with pang-…-na
items: The lemes forms use the lemes word: **pangsaéna** (*saé*), **pangageungna** (*ageung*).
Abdi ____ teu terang. (well, as for me)
Ieu ____ naon? (what is this thing, then)
Buku ____ mana? (the book we were talking about)

exercises.prompt: Choose the right intensifier: pisan, teuing, rada, or mani.
items: Complaining the sambal is too hot: Lada ____.
The price is a little higher than expected: ____ awis.
Too much, you can't finish it: Seueur ____.

exercises.prompt: Translate into Sundanese, using a suitable particle.
items: Oh, there is one after all!
Oh, come on, don't be like that.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

answers: mah — téh — mah — téh — mah — téh
pisan — teuing — rada — mani — teuing — pisan
Abdi mah nembé sumping. — Aya geuning! — Hayu atuh, ulah kitu. — Ieu waé, nu pangmurahna. — Duka teuing. — Awis, tebih deuih.
Abdi mah teu terang. — Ieu téh naon? — Hayu atuh ka warung. — Ieu waé nu pangmurahna. — Duka teuing, euy.
